description: Width tiers for Languages — F-10 sequence, Year 1-2 band. All standards are capability descriptors. C strand standards use task_contexts as the primary width axis. U strand standards use phenomena_contexts (Systems of language and Language and culture). At this band students move from supported recognition to modelled production across a range of personal and classroom contexts.
subject: Languages

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single task context or phenomenon that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For C strand: minimum is the narrowest communicative context in which the described interaction, mediation or creation is genuine — not modelled repetition without communicative intent. For U strand: minimum is engagement with the described language feature in at least one familiar context with evidence of understanding.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. For C strand: a range of task types and communicative contexts that reflect the descriptor's full interactional or creative intent. For U strand: the range of language features and cultural connections described in the elaborations.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new communicative contexts, cultural communities, comparison languages or task types. Width adds breadth of context — not difficulty of the same task. For U strand: additional language features, languages for comparison, or cultural contexts that deepen language awareness without exceeding the year band.
width_notes.elaborations: Target language (F-10 sequence) elaborations were used as the primary source. All target-language-specific vocabulary and grammar examples have been genericised. Elaborations are preserved verbatim in each standard entry as source record.

AC9LS2C01.minimum_width: Respond correctly to at least three classroom routine exchanges (greeting, roll call, instruction) using appropriate target language or action; produce a personal introduction with at least two elements using modelled sentence structures.
AC9LS2C01.typical_width: Participate in regular classroom routines — time-appropriate greetings, roll call, weather, day and date, classroom commands — and use modelled sentence structures to introduce themselves with name, age, family members and likes/dislikes. Ask and respond to simple personal questions. Use formulaic expressions for thanks, apologies and encouragement across familiar contexts.
wider: Initiate a greeting or personal exchange independently using the appropriate register without teacher prompting
Explain to a peer or family member the meaning of two or three classroom routine expressions and when they are used
Conduct a short question-and-answer exchange with a partner across at least two different personal topics without relying on a single rehearsed script
elaborations: greeting and farewelling each other according to the time of the day and relationship to the person
participating in regular class routines such as stating the weather, the day and date, how they feel and making announcements
responding to simple classroom instructions and roll call
following classroom commands and imperatives using actions and gestures
following teacher instructions to complete activities or build/draw an imaginary character
introducing and describing themselves using modelled sentence structures and visual supports
using modelled statements to express likes and dislikes
using formulaic language to express thanks, apologies, praise and well wishes
asking and responding to questions using modelled sentences to discuss their personal worlds
requesting permission or seeking approval from peers using modelled expressions

AC9LS2C02.minimum_width: Participate in at least two activity types (e.g. a structured game and a song) using target language expressions appropriate to each; use at least one spontaneous expression during a game or activity.
AC9LS2C02.typical_width: Participate in a range of guided, play-based language activities — games involving turn-taking and matching, songs and chants with gesture, short role-plays using props, and collaborative class tasks. Use spontaneous formulaic expressions during activities. Use digital tools collaboratively for language tasks.
wider: Lead a familiar game or song in the target language — calling out instructions or leading a chant for classmates
Participate in a role-play or collaborative task that introduces an element not previously rehearsed — applying known language flexibly to a new activity context
Create a new version of a familiar game by substituting target language vocabulary — demonstrating creative application of known language
elaborations: participating in games or activities that involve taking turns, suggesting, making choices or swapping/matching items
using spontaneous expressions, phrases and non-verbal communication when playing games or engaging in activities
exchanging, sorting and classifying objects and attributes using simple question forms and affirmative/negative responses
taking part in short role-plays or skits using spoken and visual cues, props and realia
contributing to class activities or projects such as making a birthday calendar or weather board
reciting and performing chants, songs and rhymes using gestures such as clapping or dancing
using digital tools or applications collaboratively in pairs or groups to enhance learning

AC9LS2C03.minimum_width: Identify at least three key words or phrases in a familiar text using context, pictures or intonation as support; demonstrate comprehension through at least one appropriate response (labelling, matching, drawing or selecting).
AC9LS2C03.typical_width: Locate key information in a range of familiar spoken, written and digital texts — stories, songs, rhymes, simple dialogues — using pictures, keywords and contextual clues. Respond to texts through varied modes: play-acting, illustrating, movement, verbal response. Categorise information from texts using simple graphic organisers. Respond to questions about characters, places and objects.
wider: Sequence events from a familiar text using images or key words — demonstrating comprehension beyond isolated word recognition
Compare the use of gesture and body language in target language texts with gesture conventions from the student's own language background
Create a bilingual graphic organiser from a text — categorising information in both target language and English and identifying at least one cognate
elaborations: listening for and identifying key words and phrases in a range of simple texts, using intonation patterns to assist understanding
participating in shared reading of print and digital texts using pictures, keywords and contextual clues to predict meaning
demonstrating comprehension by labelling, matching, drawing, miming or onscreen pointing, clicking or dragging

recognising that gestures and body language are integral to communicating in language for First Nations Australians, and showing examples of how they are also integral to communicating in the target language
participating in shared class stories and responding to and repeating keywords
listening to, reading or viewing adapted versions of familiar stories and incorporating recurring keywords and expressions
responding to questions about people, places and objects
responding to spoken, print or digital texts through play-acting, illustrating or movement
categorising information using graphic organisers such as drawings or simple tables

AC9LS2C04.minimum_width: Identify at least two target language greetings or address forms and explain what relationship or context each signals.
AC9LS2C04.typical_width: Notice that target language greetings, forms of address and expressions carry cultural meaning — that choices signal relationship, respect and context. Compare formal and informal address forms. Notice body language, tone and cultural expressions in target language interaction. Create resources (word walls, bilingual dictionaries) explaining cultural terms.
wider: Explain a target language greeting or address convention to someone outside the classroom — articulate what the convention means and why it matters
Compare non-verbal communication conventions in target language and English contexts — identify at least one gesture or body language convention that differs
Explore expressions in Australian English that carry cultural meaning (e.g. g'day, ta) and compare with target language equivalents — identify what each set reveals about cultural priorities
elaborations: recognising the cultural significance of hand gestures and facial expressions that accompany words and phrases in the target language
explaining to others the meanings and use of simple expressions such as greetings used for different times of day, occasions and people
noticing body language and tone when using some target language words, expressions and exclamations
making class word walls or personal bilingual picture dictionaries with captions and simple descriptions to explain cultural terms
understanding that different forms of language are used with different people to show respect and familiarity, and that there may be regional variations

AC9LS2C05.minimum_width: Create a text about themselves with at least three target language elements using modelled structures; produce at least one written or multimodal element (label, caption, speech bubble) alongside spoken text.
AC9LS2C05.typical_width: Use familiar words, phrases and modelled language to create spoken, written and multimodal texts across personal and imaginative purposes — self-portraits, character descriptions, bilingual greeting cards, story re-enactments, simple captions and labels. Substitute words to create adapted versions of known songs or stories. Create texts for real communicative purposes (celebrations, displays, school events).
wider: Create a bilingual text (target language and English) about themselves or a familiar topic — identifying where structures are parallel and where they differ
Substitute multiple elements to create a genuinely adapted version of a known story or song — changing character, setting and at least one action
Create a multimodal text for a genuine audience outside the classroom — a greeting card, display caption, or event announcement — making deliberate language choices for the recipient
elaborations: creating a self-portrait or short profile using simple statements and familiar vocabulary
creating, describing or acting out real or imaginary characters using formulaic language and supporting pictures
colouring in flags and adding labels or words in cloze exercises, then creating a personal flag with description
matching bilingual captions/labels to images of First Nations Country/Place locations
using digital tools to create informative multimodal texts such as e-books, animations, videos, voice overs or captions
adding bilingual captions or speech bubbles to a photographic display or newsletter article
making bilingual greeting cards for celebrations using greetings alongside equivalent English greetings
using key words and phrases to describe aspects of a video clip or photo story
substituting words to create alternative versions of well-known stories, songs or rhymes
labelling target language communities on a map and creating descriptions using modelled language

AC9LS2U01.minimum_width: Correctly produce all target language vowel sounds in familiar words; imitate at least two target language sounds not present in English with adequate accuracy for recognition.
AC9LS2U01.typical_width: Recognise and imitate the sounds and rhythms of the target language — including vowel sounds, consonant combinations not present in English, silent letters, and statement/question intonation distinctions. Participate in alphabet songs and games. Develop rhythm and pace through songs, chants and movement activities. Use onomatopoeic words in context.
wider: Explain the difference between at least two target language sounds and their nearest English approximations — demonstrating metalinguistic awareness of the phonological difference
Perform a familiar chant or song with deliberate attention to rhythm, stress and pace — demonstrating prosodic control beyond word-level accuracy
Compare target language and English animal sounds or onomatopoeia — identify where the conventions differ and discuss what this reveals about the two languages
elaborations: becoming familiar with the sounds of the alphabet in the target language, noticing any letters not found in English
imitating target language sounds that do not exist in English
recognising that some sounds in the target language do not exist in English, so they may be challenging to pronounce
recognising and applying target language vowel sounds and vowel-consonant combinations
identifying additional consonants and digraphs in the target language and experimenting with tongue positioning
listening to familiar vocabulary and identifying silent letters
noticing that statements and questions have different intonation
developing pronunciation, phrasing and intonation skills by singing, reciting and repeating words in context
experimenting with sounds in onomatopoeic words related to animal sounds and actions

AC9LS2U02.minimum_width: Use the correct article form with at least four familiar nouns; produce at least two noun phrases with correct adjective placement and gender/class agreement.
AC9LS2U02.typical_width: Recognise how the target language uses the Roman alphabet and grammatical features to construct meaning — including noun class/gender signalled by articles, adjective placement and agreement, basic verb forms, simple affirmative and negative statements, possessive adjectives, and key punctuation differences from English. Use numbers for age, dates and time.
wider: Sort a set of unfamiliar target language nouns into grammatical categories using endings and context clues — explain the pattern applied
Produce three or four connected sentences about a topic — demonstrating early sentence-level composition beyond isolated statements
Compare the punctuation of a target language and English sentence — identify every difference and explain it
elaborations: differentiating the alphabet used in the target language from other alphabets or scripts
using numbers for simple ideas such as telling the time, expressing age and dates, and playing games
noticing that the personal pronoun can be omitted in the target language
noticing that adjectives usually follow nouns (or vary from English placement) and are used to describe characteristics
noticing endings of simple verbs and using them in modelled and formulaic expressions
making connections between articles and word endings to understand that nouns may have a grammatical class or gender
observing gender/class in patterns of naming and using singular forms of nouns and adjectives
observing capitalisation differences between the target language and English
learning the structure of simple affirmative and negative statements
identifying basic punctuation marks that differ from English
recognising and using definite and indefinite articles with nouns
using singular possessive adjectives to show ownership

AC9LS2U03.minimum_width: Identify at least three target language-English cognates and explain what makes them recognisable; identify at least one structural difference between the target language and English with a supporting example.
AC9LS2U03.typical_width: Notice and describe features of the target language that are similar to or different from English — including cognates (with possible pronunciation differences), plural forms, grammatical gender absent in English, adjective placement, punctuation differences, and words borrowed between the two languages. Create bilingual comparison texts identifying similarities and differences.
wider: Find target language-English cognates independently and test whether their meaning is truly equivalent — identify any false friends
Compare a familiar target language text with its English equivalent — list every textual difference noticed (language, structure, characters, conventions)
Find examples of target language words used in Australian English and English words used in the target language — explain what the borrowing pattern reveals about how languages influence each other
elaborations: observing features of familiar types of texts such as stories and greeting cards, and comparing them with English equivalents
understanding grammatical features present in the target language but absent in English (e.g. grammatical gender, different word order)
noticing plural forms similar to or different from English
noticing there are cognates in the target language and English, but pronunciation may differ
creating an identity card with parallel personal information in the target language and English, noticing similarities and differences
comparing how target language words used in Australian English are pronounced by speakers of each language
noticing the differences between punctuation marks in the target language and English
identifying words in the target language borrowed from other languages, and vice versa

AC9LS2U04.minimum_width: Identify at least two target language communities on a world map; identify at least one way language use varies between target language communities; identify that First Nations Australians have languages connected to their Country.
AC9LS2U04.typical_width: Notice that people use language in ways that reflect cultural practices — exploring target language community diversity, formal/informal address, cultural symbols and traditions, and the relationship between language and identity. Engage with First Nations Australian language connections to place. Recognise that some people speak more than one language and that the student belongs to multiple communities.
wider: Research one specific target language community — find two or three cultural practices reflected in the language used there and share findings
Find one local First Nations place name and research its meaning — connect this to the idea that language carries the history and identity of a community
Compare the student's own ways of expressing cultural identity (language, practices, terms) with a target language community's ways — find at least one meaningful similarity and one difference
elaborations: identifying terms and concepts that can be used to help understand and discuss culture
locating target language communities on a world map and understanding that culture varies greatly among these places
recognising that the target language is an important world language spoken in different forms in many countries
exploring symbols and languages used by First Nations Australians and by target language communities in a range of contexts
noticing aspects of the lives of children in target language communities as represented in print and digital images, stories and video
comparing their own ways of communicating and making meaning, including using any other language(s) they may speak
identifying formal and informal language use between people in different contexts
noticing expressions and terms used in Australian English that reflect lifestyles and culture
identifying themselves as belonging to different groups such as family, community, class or peer groups
discussing how colours or animals can represent different meanings and identity across cultures
